bullets.text: Machine Learning (ML) is a subfield of Artificial Intelligence (AI).
ML systems learn patterns from data rather than being explicitly programmed.
Models improve over time with more data without needing reprogramming.
It's about teaching computers to learn from experience, like humans.

sections.heading: The Ubiquity and Importance of ML

bullets.text: Machine learning is integrated into many aspects of daily life.
Examples include Netflix recommendations, spam filters, and virtual assistants.
Also used in facial recognition, online shopping, and fraud detection systems.
Access to vast amounts of data from various sources (social media, web searches).
Increased computational power, especially with modern GPUs.
Development of sophisticated algorithms capable of extracting insights.
Most common type, trains models using labeled data (input + correct output).
Model learns input-output relationships to predict new outputs.
Example: Predicting house prices based on features and actual sale prices.
Categories: Regression (predicting continuous values) and Classification (predicting discrete labels).
Uses unlabeled data, with no explicit answers provided.
Goal is for the algorithm to discover patterns or structures independently.
Application: Clustering, like grouping customers by buying behavior.
Application: Dimensionality reduction to simplify data with many features.
An agent learns by interacting with an environment.
Receives feedback as rewards or penalties, adjusting strategy to maximize total reward.
Example: Training a robot to walk or an AI to play games like chess.
Used in robotics, game-playing AI (AlphaGo), and self-driving cars.
Data quality: Noisy, biased, or incomplete data degrades model performance.
Overfitting: Model learns training data too well, failing to generalize to new data.
Ethical concerns: Biased data can lead to biased models with serious real-world consequences.
Requires understanding data, context, and the impact of models.
Recap of ML definition, importance, types, and challenges.
Future lectures will explore algorithms and practical applications in depth.
